title: Potawatomi fire-keepers and the Ohio Valley wars
summary: The Potawatomi, “keepers of the fire,” had no towns in Kentucky but joined the Northwest alliance that fought American settlement along the Ohio.
bodyMarkdown:
The [Potawatomi](https://grokipedia.com/page/Potawatomi) call themselves Bodéwadmi, often translated "keepers of the fire." They are an Anishinaabe people of the western Great Lakes. With the Ojibwe and the Odawa they form the [Council of Three Fires](https://grokipedia.com/page/Council_of_Three_Fires), an old alliance in which the Potawatomi were said to keep the council fire.

Their towns stood around Green Bay, along the St. Joseph River in southwest Michigan, at Chicago and Milwaukee, and later across northern Indiana and Illinois. None was in Kentucky. They did not hunt here the way the Shawnee and Lenape did.

Their Kentucky tie came through war. After the Revolution, the nations north of the Ohio formed a loose confederacy to stop American settlement from crossing the river. Potawatomi warriors joined it, fighting beside Shawnee, Miami, Lenape, Wyandot, and their Odawa and Ojibwe kin. The fight is called the [Northwest Indian War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northwest_Indian_War).

Kentucky men were in that war from the start. In June 1791, Kentucky volunteers under Brig. Gen. [Charles Scott](/people/#charles-scott) struck Wea and Kickapoo towns on the Wabash. Scott's report names no Potawatomi town. That November, the confederacy crushed Gen. [Arthur St. Clair](/people/#arthur-st-clair)'s army in Ohio, and Potawatomi warriors were part of that victory. Many Kentucky militiamen died in that defeat.

The tide turned in August 1794, when Gen. [Anthony Wayne](/people/#anthony-wayne), with Kentucky mounted volunteers under Scott, won at [Fallen Timbers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Fallen_Timbers). The next summer the Potawatomi were among the nations that signed the [Treaty of Greenville](/stories/treaty-of-greenville-1795-the-line-to-the-kentucky-river/). That treaty ended most raiding across the Ohio and made life safer in Kentucky's northern counties.

For the Potawatomi it was the start of a long loss of land. Treaties over the next forty years took most of their country. In 1838 Indiana Potawatomi were forced west on a march remembered as the Trail of Death.

The stories of the [Odawa](/stories/egushawa-and-the-odawa-in-kentuckys-war-years/) and the [Kickapoo](/stories/kickapoo-on-the-kentucky-frontier/) tell more of that same alliance.

## Kentucky today

No Potawatomi site is known in Kentucky. The nation lives on in several federally recognized tribes, among them the Citizen Potawatomi Nation in Oklahoma, the Prairie Band in Kansas, the Forest County Potawatomi in Wisconsin, and the Pokagon Band in Michigan.
Source: [Grokipedia: Potawatomi](https://grokipedia.com/page/Potawatomi)
